physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: A patient is ready to stand from the wheelchair for gait as the PT directed. How should the aide use the gait belt?

options.a: Buckle it snugly around the chair back to keep the patient seated until the PT arrives
options.b: Loop it under both axillae and hoist the patient's full body weight to standing
options.c: Use it instead of the ordered walker so the patient's hands stay free during gait
options.d: Fasten it at the waist as trained and use it to guide, not to lift full weight

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: A gait belt is a handling aid for transfer or gait you were trained to perform. It goes around the waist (or as fitted) so you can steady and guide. It is not a restraint, not a full-body hoist, and it does not replace an ordered walker or cane.

distractorExplanations.a: Buckling a gait belt to a chair to hold someone seated is restraint use, not an assistive transfer skill.
distractorExplanations.b: A belt guides and steadies; a full lift needs a mechanical lift or enough trained staff, not an axillary hoist.
distractorExplanations.c: The belt does not replace the walker or other device the PT ordered for balance and weight bearing.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: You are about to help a patient stand from a wheelchair for a short walk the PT set up. What must you do before the sit-to-stand?

options.a: Lock both wheelchair brakes, explain the steps, and use the ordered belt or device
options.b: Have the patient yank up on the walker while you hold one forearm only
options.c: Leave the brakes unlocked so the chair can roll with the patient's first step
options.d: Stand behind the chair and lift the patient under both axillae into standing

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: An unlocked wheelchair rolls away as the patient stands and is a common fall setup. Lock the brakes, position the chair, explain the sequence, and use the gait belt and assistive device the PT ordered. Patients push from the armrests; they do not pull the walker over onto themselves.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulling on walker handles tips the frame toward the patient; they should push up from locked armrests instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Unlocked brakes let the chair slide back during sit-to-stand and dump the patient onto the floor.
distractorExplanations.d: Axillary lifts injure shoulders; use a gait belt and the transfer method you were shown.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: During standing balance at the parallel bars, the patient says the room is spinning and looks pale. What should the aide do first?

options.a: Keep the patient walking at a brisk pace so blood pressure rises on its own
options.b: Lower the patient to sitting or the floor as trained and call the clinician
options.c: Hold the patient upright at the bars until the dizziness passes on its own
options.d: Hand a cup of water while the patient stays standing to finish the remaining set

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Near-syncope is a fall and medical-risk moment. Lower the patient safely to a chair or the floor using the method you were trained for, stay with them, and notify the PT or covering clinician. Do not keep them upright, keep walking, or treat it as a hydration break while they stand.

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing to walk while faint increases the chance of a collapse; sit or lower first, then get the clinician.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding someone upright through dizziness still risks syncope and an uncontrolled fall at the bars.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluids do not treat acute near-syncope; remaining standing to drink delays a safe lower and a clinical check.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: The next gym patient needs a gait-belt transfer and has no isolation order on the chart. Which infection-control step is correct?

options.a: Skip gloves unless the chart already names a known resistant organism
options.b: Keep the same pair of gloves on for every gym patient until they tear
options.c: Use hand hygiene and gloves whenever contact with body fluids is likely
options.d: Use alcohol gel instead of gloves if you will touch a draining wound

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Standard precautions apply to every patient, not only those with a listed infection. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves when you may contact blood, drainage, urine, or other body fluids, then change gloves and clean hands between patients. Extra transmission-based steps are added when the clinician or chart specifies them.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a named MDRO confuses standard precautions with isolation; fluids from any patient can carry pathogens.
distractorExplanations.b: One pair of gloves for a whole gym block spreads microbes; change gloves and clean hands between patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Sanitizer does not replace gloves for expected contact with wound drainage or other body fluids.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: You notice a puddle on the gym floor between the parallel bars and the mats. What should you do?

options.a: Leave it for housekeeping to mop after the last patient of the afternoon
options.b: Keep treating if every patient in the bay is already wearing non-skid socks
options.c: Walk patients across it as long as a gait belt is already fastened on them
options.d: Stop traffic, dry or mark the spill now, and keep patients off that path

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: A wet gym floor is an immediate slip hazard for patients who already have balance or gait limits. Block the path, dry or cone it, and call housekeeping as needed. Non-skid socks and a gait belt do not make a puddle safe to cross.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting until end of shift leaves the puddle in the treatment path; staff must control it as soon as it is seen.
distractorExplanations.b: Grip socks reduce but do not remove slip risk on standing water, especially with an assistive device.
distractorExplanations.c: A gait belt helps you guard a fall; it does not dry the floor or make the crossing safe.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: The PT has you guard a patient on stairs with a gait belt as you were shown. Where should you stand?

options.a: Stay below the patient so you can control a fall: behind going up, in front going down
options.b: Stand on the step above the patient when they are descending the flight
options.c: Walk two steps ahead when they are going up so you can set the stepping pace
options.d: Drop the gait belt on the landing so they can rest without you holding on

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: On stairs you guard from the downhill side so you can block a fall rather than be pulled down with the patient. That means behind and slightly below on ascent, in front and below on descent, with a secure gait-belt hold the whole time, including landings.

distractorExplanations.b: Standing above a descending patient puts you uphill of a fall; you cannot control the drop from there.
distractorExplanations.c: Walking ahead on the way up leaves you above the patient; guard from behind and below as trained.
distractorExplanations.d: Landings are a frequent loss-of-balance point; keep the gait belt in hand through the rest stop.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: A patient is postoperative day 2 after a posterior total hip. The written precaution sheet is on the chart. What should the aide do during the transfer?

options.a: Seat them in a low, soft couch so the operative hip feels more comfortable
options.b: Keep flexion, adduction, and crossing limits exactly as the clinician listed
options.c: Let them cross the operative ankle over the other knee if that feels natural
options.d: Skip the ordered raised toilet seat so the transfer looks more like home height

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Hip precautions are a clinician order, not an aide judgment call. Follow the listed limits (commonly avoiding excess flexion, adduction, and internal rotation after a posterior approach) and use the equipment ordered, such as a raised seat. Do not invent range or drop devices to make the transfer 'more normal.'

distractorExplanations.a: A deep, soft seat often flexes the hip past the listed limit and is a typical posterior-precaution trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Crossing the legs adducts and can internally rotate the hip, which many posterior protocols forbid.
distractorExplanations.d: A raised seat is ordered to limit flexion; skipping it to mimic home height violates the written precaution.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: A patient on portable oxygen is walking with a rolling walker. The tubing is looping under a walker wheel. What should the aide do?

options.a: Pull the tubing taut from the tank so none of the line can drag on the floor
options.b: Ignore the loop because wheeled walkers usually roll over tubing without catching
options.c: Stop, clear the tubing from the path, and keep slack from catching a wheel
options.d: Have the patient step on the loop so it stays pinned away from the wheels

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Oxygen tubing is a trip and equipment hazard during gait. Stop, pick the line out of the walker path, and manage slack so it cannot wrap a wheel or yank the cannula. Do not yank it taut, ignore it, or pin it under a foot.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling the line taut can dislodge the cannula or snag the walker; manage slack, do not stretch it.
distractorExplanations.b: Wheels catch tubing as easily as posts; rolling walkers still need line management.
distractorExplanations.d: Stepping on tubing can trip the patient or kink flow; it is not a way to park the line.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: The plan of care calls for a mechanical lift, and you have not been checked off on that device. What should you do?

options.a: Ask a coworker to talk you through the buttons while you operate the lift
options.b: Estimate a sling size from the patient's height and complete one transfer
options.c: Have a family member run the controls while you hold the edges of the sling
options.d: Stop and get a trained staff member; do not operate an untrained lift

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Mechanical lifts drop patients when slings, clips, or boom controls are used incorrectly. If you are not trained and competency-checked on that lift, do not operate it. Get staff who are checked off. Verbal coaching, guessed sling size, or family at the controls is not a substitute for training.

distractorExplanations.a: A hallway briefing is not competency; untrained operators still mis-hook slings and boom controls.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong sling size or attachment can dump the patient; sizing follows the device instructions, not a height guess.
distractorExplanations.c: Family members are not trained operators; licensed staff remain responsible for the lift.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: The PT's order is NWB left lower extremity. On the walk to the bathroom the patient asks to 'just put a little weight' on the toes. What should the aide do?

options.a: Keep the left foot off the floor as ordered; do not advance weight bearing
options.b: Allow toe-touch for balance only, because that still counts as no real weight
options.c: Let them bear as much as feels comfortable if they keep both hands on the walker
options.d: Permit partial weight through the walker because PWB is close enough to NWB

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: NWB means that limb takes no weight—no foot-flat, no toe-touch, no 'just a little.' TTWB/TDWB, PWB, and WBAT are different orders. An aide does not independently progress weight bearing because the patient asks or because a walker is in use. Follow the written status and tell the PT if the patient cannot stay NWB.

distractorExplanations.b: Toe-touch is TTWB/TDWB, a different order; NWB allows no contact that loads the limb.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight bearing as tolerated is WBAT; a walker does not convert NWB into a comfort-based load.
distractorExplanations.d: Partial weight bearing is PWB with a stated percent or limit; the aide cannot upgrade NWB to PWB.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: You just finished a transfer that required gloves. The gloves are off. What is required next?

options.a: Skip washing if your hands look clean and the gloves did not tear during the transfer
options.b: Perform hand hygiene now, even if the gloves looked intact when you removed them
options.c: Wash only if you see soil or the patient already had a listed infection on the chart
options.d: Rub lotion on instead of soap or gel so your skin stays intact for the next patient

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Gloves leak and contaminate the hands during removal. Hand hygiene is required after every glove removal, not only when soil is visible or when the patient is on isolation. Lotion is not a substitute for soap or alcohol gel.

distractorExplanations.a: Clean-looking hands after intact gloves still need hygiene; unseen leaks and doffing contamination are common.
distractorExplanations.c: Visible soil or a named infection is not the threshold; hygiene follows every glove removal.
distractorExplanations.d: Lotion may go on after hands are clean; it does not kill or remove microbes in place of hygiene.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: A patient drops to the mat and begins a generalized seizure during mat work. What should the aide do?

options.a: Hold both arms and legs still so the jerking cannot cause a fracture
options.b: Slide a padded bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
options.c: Protect the head, clear hazards, time the event, and get help now
options.d: Sit them up and offer sips of water as soon as the shaking starts to slow

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: During a seizure, protect the person from nearby equipment, cushion the head, time the event, and call for the clinician or emergency response per policy. Do not restrain limbs, put objects in the mouth, or give fluids. After it stops, recovery position and airway watch follow facility first-aid steps.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing limbs still during clonic movement can cause injury; clear the area instead of restraining.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing goes in the mouth; bite blocks and fingers break teeth and can block the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluids during or right after a seizure risk aspiration; keep them on the side, not sitting to drink.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: A patient with diabetes used a lancet in the gym restroom and asks you to throw it away. Where does it go?

options.a: Recap the lancet by hand, then drop it in the nearest open trash can
options.b: Drop it into a red biohazard bag hanging on the linen hamper
options.c: Wrap it in a paper towel and seal it inside a regular trash bag
options.d: Place it immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Used lancets and needles go in a rigid, labeled sharps container at the point of use. Bags tear, trash cans are not puncture-resistant, and recapping by hand is a classic needlestick. Diabetes supplies follow the same sharps rule as any other sharp.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping causes needlesticks; used lancets go uncapped into a sharps box, not the trash.
distractorExplanations.b: Biohazard bags are for some regulated waste but they puncture; sharps need a hard container.
distractorExplanations.c: Paper and plastic bags are not puncture-resistant; housekeeping can be stuck through the bag.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: You are transferring a patient from a hospital gown onto a mat in a shared gym bay. How do you protect privacy?

options.a: Close the curtain or door as appropriate before exposing the patient
options.b: Leave the bay open so any staff walking by can step in quickly to help
options.c: Review the diagnosis out loud so nearby patients know why the transfer is slow
options.d: Skip the extra gown or drape so the transfer takes less time on the mat

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: Transfers often expose skin or a gown gap. Close the curtain or door, drape as needed, and keep diagnosis talk off the open gym floor. Privacy is part of safe, respectful care; speed is not a reason to skip it. Call extra hands in without leaving the patient on display.

distractorExplanations.b: An open bay exposes the patient; staff can be called in without leaving the space uncovered.
distractorExplanations.c: Discussing the diagnosis in a shared gym is a confidentiality breach, not a courtesy to neighbors.
distractorExplanations.d: Dropping the drape to save time exposes the patient and does not make the transfer safer.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.prompt: While you are guarding, the patient loses balance and ends up on the floor. What should you do?

options.a: Lift them straight back into the chair by yourself before anyone else sees
options.b: Stay with them, call for help per policy, and do not haul them up alone
options.c: Help them stand if they say they feel fine and want to keep walking now
options.d: Finish the remaining exercises first, then write the fall in the chart later

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-sa.explanation: After a fall, stay with the patient, protect them from further injury, and get help per facility policy so a clinician can assess before they stand. Do not lift them alone, accept 'I feel fine' as clearance, or delay reporting. Document after the patient is safe and assessed.

distractorExplanations.a: A solo lift can worsen a fracture or head injury and is not a substitute for the fall-response policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients often do not feel an injury at once; the clinician assesses before they return to standing.
distractorExplanations.d: Finishing the session delays assessment and reporting; falls are handled immediately, then documented.
